extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on use, authorship, formalities, evidentiary content, and substantive standards for affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131(a)/(b) to antedate prior art and overcome pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit may overcome non-commensurate claim if obvious variations shown
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if applicant’s 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit is not fully commensurate with the rejected claim, the applicant can still overcome the rejection by showing that the differences between the claimed invention and the showing under 37 CFR 1.131(a) would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art, in view of applicant’s 37 CFR 1.131(a) evidence, prior to the effective date of the reference(s) or the activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The affidavit/declaration must still establish possession of the invention by the inventor (i.e., the basic inventive concept) and not just of what one reference happens to show if that reference does not itself teach the basic inventive concept. (Example: In re Spiller — affidavit established use of electrostatic forces in another context and was sufficient because prior art showed related deposition techniques.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Swearing behind combined references (plurality) — possession requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection based on a combination of references by showing completion of the invention by the inventor prior to the effective date of any of the references; applicant need not antedate the reference with the earliest prior art date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, the 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit must show possession by the inventor of either the whole invention as claimed or something falling within the claim(s) before the prior art date of the reference being antedated; it is not enough merely to show possession of what the reference happens to show if the reference does not teach the basic inventive concept. Where Reference A is applied in view of Reference B, teachings of Reference B may be used to show obviousness of differences before Reference A's date, but the affidavit must still establish inventor's possession of the claimed invention (not just what Reference A shows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antedating generic claims by showing a single species
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference or activity applied against generic claims may (in most cases) be antedated as to such claims by an affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(a) showing completion of the invention of only a single species, within the genus, before the prior art date of the reference or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions where predictability is in question (unpredictable arts): see MPEP § 715.03. The affidavit must show as much as the minimum disclosure required by a patent specification to furnish support for a generic claim; where predictability is low, one or a few species may not suffice to infer generic applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species claim antedating rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claim under rejection recites a species and the reference or activity discloses the claimed species, the rejection can be overcome under 37 CFR 1.131(a) directly by showing prior completion of the claimed species or indirectly by a showing of prior completion of a different species coupled with a showing that the claimed species would have been an obvious modification of the species completed by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: In re Spiller. Applicant may rely on prior completion of a different species if it would have rendered the claimed species obvious to a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claim antedating rules and multi-species disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure of a species in a cited reference is generally sufficient to prevent a later applicant from obtaining a generic claim. If the only pertinent disclosure in the reference is a single species, the applicant can overcome the rejection by showing prior possession of the species disclosed. If the reference discloses several species of a claimed genus, the applicant can overcome the reference directly only by showing that the inventor completed, prior to the date of the reference or activity, all of the species shown in the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively, proof of prior completion of a species different from the species of the reference will be sufficient indirectly if the species shown in the reference would have been obvious in view of the species shown to have been made by the inventor. The test is whether the species completed by the inventor provided an adequate basis for inferring that the invention has generic applicability. (Cited cases: In re Gosteli; In re Plumb; In re Clarke; In re Rainer; In re Shokal.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Species versus embodiments distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: References or activities which disclose one or more embodiments of a single claimed invention can be overcome by filing a 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit showing prior completion of a single embodiment of the invention, whether it is the same or a different embodiment from that disclosed in the reference or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In contrast, in genus/species disclosures, it is necessary that species reduced to practice provide an adequate basis for inferring that the invention has generic applicability. (Example: In re Fong: multiple detergents were embodiments of same invention rather than species of a genus.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may make an affidavit or declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations filed under 37 CFR 1.131 to overcome a rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 must be made by either: (A) the entire inventive entity (i.e., the inventor); (B) less than all named joint inventors if it is shown that less than all named joint inventors invented the subject matter of the claim(s) under rejection; (C)-(F) various pre-AIA provisions allow joint inventors, assignees, legal representatives, or assignees/parties in interest in certain circumstances; (G) owner during reexamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For applications filed before Sept. 16, 2012 where a named joint inventor is unavailable, remaining joint inventors may sign provided a petition under 37 CFR 1.183 requesting waiver of the signature is submitted with proof that non-signing inventor is unavailable. See MPEP § 409.03(d) and Office of Petitions procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements of affidavits and declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit is a statement in writing made under oath before a notary public or other authorized officer. 37 CFR 1.68 permits a declaration to be used instead of an affidavit; the declaration must include an acknowledgment that willful false statements are punishable (18 U.S.C. 1001) and a statement that statements of the declarant's own knowledge are true and that statements made on information and belief are believed to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 602 for additional formal requirements. Declarations must include the specified criminal false-statement acknowledgment and the declarant's attestation regarding knowledge and belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations when reference is a U.S. patent or application publication claiming same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A 37 CFR 1.131(a) affidavit is ineffective to overcome a United States patent or patent application publication that claims the same invention as the application being examined (not only verbatim correspondence but also where there is no patentable distinction). If the reference claims the same invention and its publication date or issue date is within certain timeframes relative to the presentation of claims, remedies other than Rule 131 (e.g., interference under 37 CFR 41.202 or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 135(b)) may apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If commonly owned patents/applications contain claims that are identical or not patentably distinct, the subject matter is 'interfering subject matter' (37 CFR 41.203(a)). Where the reference and application are commonly owned but not patentably distinct, a terminal disclaimer and an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) may be used to overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection. Form paragraphs (¶ 23.14, ¶ 23.14.01) and MPEP Chapter 2300 and § 2159 provide additional instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts and documentary evidence requirements (exhibits and specificity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential thing to be shown under 37 CFR 1.131(a) is priority of invention and this may be done by any satisfactory evidence of the fact. FACTS, not conclusions, must be alleged. Evidence in the form of exhibits may accompany the affidavit/declaration and each exhibit relied upon should be specifically referred to in terms of what it is relied upon to show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of acceptable exhibits: attached sketches, blueprints, photographs, reproductions of notebook entries, models, supporting witness statements, testimony from an interference, documents from the discontinued Disclosure Document Program. Exhibits and models must comply with 37 CFR 1.91. A general allegation that the invention was completed prior to the reference is not sufficient; vague or general statements are insufficient. The affidavit/declaration must clearly explain which facts or data applicant is relying on to show completion prior to the particular date, and the burden of showing actual reduction of practice is on the party seeking its benefit. See In re Steed, In re NTP, Inc., In re Borkowski, In re Harry, Ex parte Ovshinsky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original exhibits and 37 CFR 1.131(b) photocopy/original requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.131(b) requires that original exhibits of drawings or records, or photocopies thereof, accompany and form part of the affidavit or declaration or their absence satisfactorily explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If originals were made and lost, their contents should be reproduced and furnished in place of originals; if relying on verbal disclosures, the witness should state as nearly as possible the language used when imparting knowledge. See Ex parte Donovan for guidance and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of dates in affidavits/declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: When alleging conception or reduction to practice prior to the effective date of the reference, the dates in the oath or declaration may be the actual dates or, if disclosure of the actual dates is not desired, the declarant may allege that the acts occurred prior to a specified date. However, the actual dates of acts relied on to establish diligence must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If dates on exhibits have been removed or blocked off, the matter of dates can be addressed in the body of the affidavit/declaration. See MPEP § 715.07(a) for diligence-related date requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three ways to show prior invention under 37 CFR 1.131(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The affidavit or declaration must state FACTS and produce documentary evidence/exhibits sufficient to show one of: (A) actual reduction to practice of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference; or (B) conception of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference coupled with due diligence from prior to the reference date to a subsequent actual reduction to practice; or (C) conception of the invention prior to the effective date of the reference coupled with due diligence from prior to the reference date to the filing date of the application (constructive reduction to practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception alone confers no rights unless followed by reasonable diligence to reduction to practice or filing. Filing constitutes a constructive reduction to practice (37 CFR 1.131). See Automatic Weighing Mach. Co. v. Pneumatic Scale Corp., and cited MPEP sections for detailed discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception, reduction to practice, utility, and corroboration standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception is the mental part of the inventive act and must be capable of proof (drawings, disclosure, model). Proof of actual reduction to practice generally requires showing the apparatus actually existed and worked for its intended purpose; in some simple devices mere construction is sufficient. Whether test results are required to establish utility depends on facts. The concepts have same meanings under 37 CFR 1.131(a) as in interference proceedings, but the rule practice is for convenience and may differ in application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences from interference practice: in interference, conception, diligence, and reduction to practice require corroboration; under 37 CFR 1.131(a) an applicant may elect to stand on their own affidavit/declaration without corroboration (Ex parte Hook). Where proof of utility is required, evidence must satisfy one of ordinary skill to a reasonable certainty. See Asahi/America, Newkirk, Sachs, In re Blake, In re Wilkinson, In re Moore, In re Eickmeyer, and MPEP § 2138.04–.06 for further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence standards and burdens of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence need not be considered unless conception prior to the reference is clearly established. Diligence comes into question only after prior conception is established. An inventor is either diligent at a given time or is not; inactivity may be excused but the record must set forth an explanation or excuse. Diligence must be judged on the particular facts of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must show evidence of facts establishing diligence (not mere allegations). The dates of acts relied on to establish diligence must be provided. Vague/general assertions about exhibits without clear explanation do not satisfy 37 CFR 1.131(b). Form paragraphs 7.59.fti or 7.63.fti may be used where insufficient evidence is included.
